name: Caernarfon Castle
label: Caernarfon Castle
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/70264991: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Caernarfon Castle' (192 m across).
notes: Edward I's UNESCO World Heritage fortress, best seen from Castle Square.

text.description:
Caernarfon Castle is a huge medieval fortress in Caernarfon, Gwynedd, north-west Wales. King Edward I began the stone castle in 1283, on a spot where a Norman motte-and-bailey castle had stood since the late 11th century. It was built on a grand scale because it was meant to be the administrative centre of north Wales. The walls are said to echo those of Constantinople, and from the outside it looks almost complete, though the buildings inside have gone and some parts were never finished. It was used for the investiture of the Prince of Wales in 1911 and again in 1969. Today it is looked after by Cadw and is part of a World Heritage Site.

For a phone photo, the appeal is the sheer mass of stone. Long, solid walls and towers fill the frame, and they sit well against open sky. Start wide, then move in for smaller details such as a tower top or the stonework. Keep your gridlines on so the long wall edges stay straight, and take a few frames at slightly different angles, as the outline looks different with every few steps you take.
text.geographic_location: The castle stands on the Caernarfon waterfront, on the peninsula between the River Seiont and the Menai Strait, right beside the old town and its walls.
text.directions_text: Head for Caernarfon town; the castle sits right beside the old town, so you should see its walls as you approach. The phone icon on the map is about 20 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full length of the walls and towers. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural, less stretched view of the castle. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out towers, battlements and stone detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 20 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a main wall or tower edge up with a vertical line so the stonework does not lean. Keep a band of sky above the towers and avoid cutting through the tops. Try one wide shot of the whole castle, then one close frame of a tower using the telephoto. If people are walking by, wait a moment: a small figure at the base shows how big the walls are.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its detail and the walls don't turn into a silhouette. If you are shooting wide, keep your phone level, as the ultra-wide lens makes tilted walls look more obvious.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, lower light that brings out the texture of the stone. Midday sun can be harsh and is often busier with visitors.

text.access_note: The castle is managed by Cadw and entry to the inside may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning and late afternoon light is usually softer and shows stonework texture better than midday sun.
Midday is often busier with visitors than early or late in the day.
The exterior walls can be photographed from the area around the stand-here point without going inside the castle.
The castle sits right beside the old town and its walls are visible as you approach.

name: Royal Welch Fusiliers Museum
label: Fusiliers Museum
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OSM N12532130016 (Royal Welch Fusiliers Museum): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Regimental museum inside the castle's Queen's Tower.

text.description:
The Royal Welch Fusiliers Museum is on the Caernarfon map, and it is the second stop. It is a good place for a record shot of your visit.

The best view is from a short step back. Switch on the gridlines so the vertical edges of the building stay straight.

The default lens (1x) gives a natural, uncluttered view of the building. If you are tight on space, the ultra-wide (0.5x) will take in more, but keep the phone level and keep people away from the edges, where they can look stretched. Once you have the wide view, move closer or use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for architectural details you can see.

This is a place to visit as well as photograph, so allow time to see what is inside. Check the official site before you go for visiting details.
text.directions_text: The phone icon on the map is about 35 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole frontage. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you cannot step back far enough. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for architectural details you can see.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 35 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the museum is in front of you and you can fit in the whole of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the vertical edges of the walls with them, so the building stands straight. Hold the phone at chest height rather than tilting it up. Leave a little space around the top and sides so you do not crop the building. Then take a second, closer shot of a detail you can see on the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its detail and colour.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the frame. On bright days around midday, expect harder shadows on the walls.

text.access_note: Check the official site before you go, as entry to the museum may be ticketed or restricted.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Midday sun on bright days tends to give harder shadows on walls.

name: Segontium
label: Segontium Roman Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ben Twthill' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Ben Twthill' (way/116734892): middle (26 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/1036780270: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Segontium Roman Fort' (358 m across).
notes: Remains of a Roman auxiliary fort above the town.

text.description:
Segontium is the Roman fort on the edge of Caernarfon, and the most important one in the north of Roman Wales. It was founded by Agricola in AD 77 or 78 and built to hold about a thousand auxiliary soldiers. Unlike the medieval castle down by the water, it stands on higher ground to the east, with a good outlook towards the Menai Strait. Today you see low stone foundations laid out on the hillside, with Snowdonia behind. Most of the foundations survive, although a main road now cuts through the site. Coins found here suggest the fort was still in use until at least the year 394.

From the top, the phone picture is a wide panorama over Caernarfon's rooftops and the castle, with the Menai Strait, Anglesey and the Snowdonia hills beyond. It is a view of the setting rather than of the fort itself, so treat it as the scene-setting shot. The fort lies to the south-east, so use this photo to show where Segontium sits in the landscape. For a closer picture of the foundations with the mountains behind, go to the fort itself. It is a short walk away, but check the official site before you go, as the gate has been found locked on at least one visit. Ben Twthill can be windy, so keep a firm grip on your phone.
text.geographic_location: Segontium is on the outskirts of Caernarfon, on higher ground east of the castle and the Seiont estuary.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop near here, so from Caernarfon town centre you reach it on foot. For Ben Twthill, use the footbridge over the main road and take the path opposite St David and St Helen's Church up to the top of the hill. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the rooftops, the Strait and the mountains. Then switch to the default lens (1x), or the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the castle or a patch of hillside.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Ben Twthill (Top of the hill, reached via the footbridge over the main road and the path opposite St David and St Helen's Church). A panoramic view over Caernarfon's rooftops and castle, the Menai Strait and Anglesey, with Snowdonia in the distance. The sources describe the town and castle rather than the Roman fort, so this is a context view, not a view of Segontium itself. Segontium is off to the south-east and is not the main subject of this view.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Keep the town and castle in the foreground, with the mountains as a backdrop. Try panorama mode, moving slowly from left to right. If you also visit the fort itself, frame the excavated stone foundations low in the picture with the Snowdonia mountains behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle or town to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. In wind, hold the phone with both hands and lean against something steady, and check the photo for blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Softer light early or late in the day usually flatters the town and hills. Clear days show Snowdonia best.

text.access_note: Ben Twthill is a public park, but for the fort itself check the official site (Cadw) before you go, as access may be restricted.
claims_not_in_sources: Softer light early or late in the day usually flatters the view.
Holding the phone with both hands and leaning on something steady reduces blur in wind.

name: Caernarfon town walls
label: Town Walls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hole In the Wall Street' (1 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'The Hole in the Wall' (pois); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Medieval walls still enclosing the old town.

text.description:
Caernarfon's town walls are easy to overlook next to the castle, which is part of their appeal. They form a nearly complete ring around the old town, built between 1283 and 1292 under Edward I at the same time as the castle. The circuit is 734 m long and includes eight towers and two medieval gatehouses. Today the walls are looked after by Cadw as part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site. This spot is a quieter view of the wall at Castle Ditch, near Hole In the Wall Street.

The walls photograph well because they are rough, weathered stonework with a lot of texture, and a close view shows how solid they are. They also carry a good story. They were badly damaged in the 1294 revolt and repaired the following year, and the town's defences later held out against Owain Glyndŵr's attacks in 1403 and 1404. Houses once crowded against the walls and hid them in many places, so a clear stretch like this is worth a few frames.

Keep the wall as your main subject. Use the line of the stonework to lead the eye along the frame, and include a doorway, a window or a passer-by for scale. If you want a wider picture afterwards, the Aber Swing Bridge shows the castle, town walls and harbour together, and Greengate Street has another stretch of wall running beside the road.
text.geographic_location: The Castle Ditch stretch of Caernarfon's town wall, near Hole In the Wall Street.
text.directions_text: Plan your own way to Caernarfon. The wall subject point is about 666 m (roughly 8 minutes on foot) to the south-east, so follow the wall on the map rather than guessing at side streets. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is narrow, so you can fit in the full height of the wall. Use the default lens (1x) for a natural view, and the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for details of the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hole In the Wall Street (the stretch where the wall runs at Castle Ditch). A close view of the town wall at Castle Ditch, seen from beside the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the wall up with the horizontal lines so it looks straight. Keep the wall filling most of the frame and let the street edge guide the eye along it. For a wider view, try the Aber Swing Bridge for the castle, walls and harbour together, or Greengate Street for another stretch of wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stone keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady with both hands, as narrow streets can be shaded.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Daylight when the sun is not directly behind the wall works best, and an early start is likely to be quieter. Check the light on the day, as narrow streets can be shaded.

text.access_note: The walls can be seen from the street, but access to the wall-walk is limited, so check the official site (Cadw) before you go.

name: Aber Swing Bridge
label: Aber Swing Bridge
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/5789995: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Aber Swing Bridge' (75 m long).
notes: Pedestrian swing bridge across the harbour with a castle view.

text.description:
Aber Swing Bridge is a footbridge across the Afon Seiont in the middle of Caernarfon, linking the foreshore with the Watergate entrance close to Caernarfon Castle. It is a plain, practical structure of concrete and steel, built in 1970 and worked by electricity, and it is about 75 metres long. That makes it a good subject for a phone photo: a long, simple line across the water, with the foreshore, the Watergate and the castle close by.

The bridge has a bit of history too. It replaced an earlier swing bridge that opened on 1 March 1900, St David's Day, and that first bridge had itself replaced a ferry. The older bridge was demolished in 1969, and a bailey bridge stood in its place for a short time before the present one arrived.

For photos, use the bridge's length. The railings and deck make natural leading lines that pull the eye along the picture, and the river gives you a clean foreground. Stand back far enough to fit the whole span in, then try a second shot closer in, with a person walking across for scale. If the castle or the Watergate area appears at the far end, keep the horizon level so the buildings do not look as if they are leaning. Watch for people moving through the frame and wait for a gap if you want a tidy picture.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Caernarfon, where the Afon Seiont meets the foreshore, just by the Watergate entrance and a short walk from Caernarfon Castle.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Caernarfon near the castle. Head for the foreshore and the Watergate side of the Afon Seiont, where the bridge crosses the river. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the bridge. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole span and the surroundings in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the bridge up along one of them so the deck and railings run cleanly across the picture. Keep the phone level, and leave a little space around the bridge rather than cutting it off at the edges. For a second shot, move closer and wait for someone to walk across for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the steelwork doesn't turn into a silhouette. Hold the phone steady with both hands, or rest your elbows on a rail or wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people on the bridge. On a still day the river may give a clearer reflection.

text.access_note: The bridge is a pedestrian footbridge in the town centre.

name: Porth yr Aur
label: Porth yr Aur
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-16).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q17738516: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The Golden Gate, a medieval town gate by the harbour.

text.description:
Porth yr Aur is the old West gate of Caernarfon's town walls, a twin-towered gatehouse with a lower, projecting barbican in front. It was once the main way into the walled town from the seaward side, and it now sits right beside the castle's defences, so the two make a natural pair in a photo. The round, crenelated towers contrast with the many-sided towers of the castle, and that difference in shape gives you something to frame.

The gate was begun in 1283, at the same time as the castle, and finished by 1292. It was badly damaged during the Welsh revolt of 1294 and then repaired. Since 1854 the building has been home to the Royal Welsh Yacht Club, and one of the cannon added in the Napoleonic period is still in place on the gate. It is part of the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to take in both towers and the barbican, and keep your phone level so the walls do not lean inwards. Then switch to the default lens (1x) or a little zoom for a tighter shot of the crenelated top and the cannon. Because the building is used by the club, treat it as a place to photograph from the outside.
text.geographic_location: On the western side of the old walled town of Caernarfon, beside the castle's defences and close to the waterfront. It forms part of the town walls.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop at this spot, so start from the centre of Caernarfon, close to the castle, and head to the western side of the old walled town, towards the waterfront. From there it is a short walk to the gate. The phone icon on the map is about 10 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the whole gatehouse, then use the default lens (1x) or telephoto/zoom (2x) for details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 10 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. You are very close, which is why the ultra-wide lens helps.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the two round towers so they are balanced either side of the centre. Include the low barbican in front to show the gate's shape. Then take a second, closer shot of the battlements and the cannon with the default lens (1x).
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly if the sky is bright so the walls keep their colour and the sky is not washed out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The building is home to the Royal Welsh Yacht Club, so it is best viewed from outside; check the official site before you go if you hope to see inside.
claims_not_in_sources: The stand-here point is a few steps from the gate and the gatehouse is about 10 m east of it.
Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
The gate can be viewed from the outside from public ground near the stand-here point.
The area is close to the waterfront and the castle, within a short walk of the town centre.
